run.question: Database connection timeouts are occurring for blue-whale app in namespace app-94

report.summary: Facts observed: Deployment blue-whale in namespace app-94 (revision 1, created 2026-11-21T07:14:20Z) runs 1/1 ready with image python:3.9-slim and env DB_HOST=postgres.app-94.svc.cluster.local, DB_PORT=5432, DB_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT=30, DB_POOL_SIZE=20; its single pod blue-whale-6bdbd444c5-bwztw is Running and ready with 0 restarts, started 2026-11-21T07:14:21Z. The Service postgres in app-94 (ClusterIP 10.96.239.39, port 5432, selector app=postgres-db) exists, but its Endpoints object has empty subsets, i.e. no backing addresses. No postgres workload appears anywhere in the cluster: the complete deployment listing (25 deployments) and statefulset listing (only alertmanager) contain none, and a pod-name scan over 33 pods returned no postgres pod; the only postgres Service in the cluster is the app-94 one. The only events in the authorized window are six Normal events at 07:14:20-07:14:21 recording the Deployment scaling ReplicaSet blue-whale-6bdbd444c5 from 0 to 1 and the pod being scheduled/created/started. The only ConfigMap in app-94 is kube-root-ca.crt. Supported hypothesis: the reported database connection timeouts are explained by the postgres Service having no endpoints, so connections to postgres.app-94.svc.cluster.local:5432 cannot be established and stall until the 30s DB_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT. Counter-evidence: blue-whale itself is not crashing or restarting, and the Service object itself declares the expected port. Not verified: any application-side timeout/error text (pod logs returned zero lines and the app code is mounted from a redacted Secret), any metric or trace evidence (Prometheus and Jaeger calls returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE for this Run), and whether a postgres workload ever existed before the window (change_history is not integrated; events exist only from 07:14:20).

claims.text: Deployment blue-whale in namespace app-94 (revision 1, created 2026-11-21T07:14:20Z, 1/1 replicas ready, image python:3.9-slim, command python /app/app.py) declares env DB_HOST=postgres.app-94.svc.cluster.local, DB_PORT=5432, DB_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT=30 and DB_POOL_SIZE=20, with /app mounted from a redacted Secret.

Pod blue-whale-6bdbd444c5-bwztw in app-94 is Running and ready, restart count 0, with no last termination state, container started 2026-11-21T07:14:21Z, owned by ReplicaSet blue-whale-6bdbd444c5 (which is owned by Deployment blue-whale).

Service postgres in namespace app-94 is a ClusterIP Service at 10.96.239.39 exposing port 5432 with targetPort 5432 and selector app=postgres-db, and the corresponding Endpoints object 'postgres' in app-94 has empty subsets, i.e. no endpoint addresses.

The cluster-wide deployment listing (25 deployments returned) contains no deployment whose pod template carries app=postgres-db; the only workload in namespace app-94 is Deployment blue-whale, and the remaining deployments are kube-system/local-path-storage and otel-demo demo components.
The cluster-wide statefulset listing returned exactly one statefulset, alertmanager in otel-demo; there is no postgres statefulset.

A name search over all pods (33 pods processed, no label filter) for postgres|pgsql|-db|db- returned only frontend-proxy-844799bcdb-pv5mn and shipping-6fc5f694db-9sq2c in otel-demo (substring matches); no postgres pod appears in the returned list.

The cluster-wide service listing (31 services) contains exactly one postgres service, app-94/postgres, so DB_HOST postgres.app-94.svc.cluster.local would resolve to a Service that has no endpoints rather than to a database running elsewhere in another namespace.

Only six events fall inside the authorized window, all Normal and all at 2026-11-21T07:14:20-07:14:21Z: Deployment blue-whale 'ScalingReplicaSet' (scaled up replica set blue-whale-6bdbd444c5 from 0 to 1), ReplicaSet blue-whale-6bdbd444c5 'SuccessfulCreate', and Pod blue-whale-6bdbd444c5-bwztw 'Scheduled', 'Pulled', 'Created', 'Started'.

Namespace app-94 exists and is Active; the cluster has no separate database namespace (namespaces returned: app-94, default, kube-node-lease, kube-public, kube-system, local-path-storage, opspilot-readonly, otel-demo).
The only ConfigMap in namespace app-94 is kube-root-ca.crt; no ConfigMap in app-94 carries settings that inject database faults, errors or delays.

blue-whale is not crash-looping or being restarted: its single pod is Running and ready with restart count 0 and no previous container instance, so the timeout symptom is not explained by a blue-whale container failure in the observed state.

The postgres Service declaration itself is consistent (port 5432 -> targetPort 5432, selector app=postgres-db), so a wrong Service port/targetPort is not what produces the empty endpoint set; the endpoints object holds no addresses at all.

The blue-whale database connection timeouts are caused by the absence of a database backend: Service app-94/postgres has no endpoints, so TCP connects from blue-whale to postgres.app-94.svc.cluster.local:5432 cannot complete and block until DB_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT=30 seconds.

Candidates for why no backend exists, none of which the evidence can distinguish: the postgres workload was never deployed in this fixture cluster, or it was deleted before the authorized window (no SuccessfulDelete event survives, and the events present start only at 2026-11-21T07:14:20Z).

Rejected: blue-whale pod crash, OOMKill or eviction as the cause of the timeouts. The pod shows no restart, no last termination state and no Evicted/OOMKilled indication; all six observed events are Normal lifecycle events.

Restore a reachable PostgreSQL backend for app-94 that matches the Service selector app=postgres-db and serves port 5432 (or point DB_HOST at the real database), then confirm the endpoints of app-94/postgres become populated and re-test connectivity from the blue-whale pod.

Add DB connect-failure logging or a readiness check on blue-whale so the timeout is visible in its own logs/metrics, since the current pod emits no log lines and exposes no error signal that could be cited.

gaps: Prometheus was unreachable for this Run: get_metric_names, execute_prometheus_instant_query, metrics_range_query and get_prometheus_target all returned status error / SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, so no application error-rate, latency, timeout-counter or kube_deployment/kube_endpoints series could be read, and no metric-based statement about blue-whale's failures is possible.

Jaeger was unreachable for this Run: traces_list_services and traces_list_operations returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, and 'blue-whale' is not among the services listed for traces_search, so no span-level error or latency evidence exists for the timeout.

Application-side timeout evidence is missing: fetch_pod_logs for blue-whale-6bdbd444c5-bwztw returned zero lines both for 2026-11-21T07:14:20Z-07:14:59Z and for the default hour, so no connection-error text was observed (a zero-line read is not proof the app logged nothing elsewhere).
The blue-whale application code is mounted from a redacted Secret volume (app-code), which cannot be read, so the connection logic and how DB_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT is applied could not be verified.

No postgres workload object exists to inspect, so there is no pod status, termination reason or owner to check for the database; whether it was ever deployed or was deleted before the window is unknown, and change_history is not an integrated source in this Run.
NetworkPolicy and ResourceQuota queries returned no objects (status no_data), so whether such objects existed earlier or could block egress to 10.96.239.39:5432 is unknown rather than ruled out.
No conclusion can be drawn about the time at which the grey failure started: the only events available begin at 2026-11-21T07:14:20Z, when the blue-whale Deployment and ReplicaSet were created.
next_steps: Deploy or restore the PostgreSQL instance for namespace app-94 with pod label app=postgres-db and port 5432, or correct DB_HOST on Deployment blue-whale.
Verify with `kubectl get endpoints postgres -n app-94` that addresses appear after the backend is running.
Confirm connectivity from the blue-whale pod to postgres.app-94.svc.cluster.local:5432 and inspect its stdout after a retry.
Re-check the Prometheus and Jaeger sources once they are reachable to quantify the timeout errors and compare with a baseline window.

content.name: database-troubleshooting
content.content:
# Database Connection Troubleshooting

## Overview
This runbook helps diagnose database connection timeout issues in Kubernetes applications.

## Investigation Steps

### 1. Check Application Status
Verify the application pods are running and review recent events:
```bash
kubectl get pods -n {namespace} -l app={app_name}
kubectl describe pod -n {namespace} -l app={app_name}
```

### 2. Review Application Logs
Look for connection errors and timeout patterns:
```bash
kubectl logs -n {namespace} -l app={app_name} --tail=50 | grep -E "(timeout|connection|ERROR)"
```

### 3. Verify Database Service
Check if the database service exists and has endpoints:
```bash
kubectl get svc -n {namespace} | grep -E "(postgres|mysql|database)"
kubectl get endpoints -n {namespace} | grep -E "(postgres|mysql|database)"
```

### 4. Test Network Connectivity
Test connectivity from application pod to database:
```bash
kubectl exec -n {namespace} $(kubectl get pod -n {namespace} -l app={app_name} -o jsonpath="{.items[0].metadata.name}") -- nc -zv {db_host} {db_port}
```

### 5. Check Database Health
Connect to database and check its status:
```bash
# For PostgreSQL
kubectl exec -n {namespace} {db_pod} -- psql -U postgres -c "SELECT 1"

# Check active connections
kubectl exec -n {namespace} {db_pod} -- psql -U postgres -c "SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity"
```

### 6. Review Connection Pool Configuration
Check application's database connection pool settings:
```bash
kubectl get deployment -n {namespace} {app_name} -o yaml | grep -A10 "env:"
```

## Common Issues

1. **No Database Endpoints**: Database service has no backing pods
2. **Connection Pool Exhaustion**: All connections in use, increase pool size
3. **Network Policy**: Check if NetworkPolicies block database access
4. **DNS Resolution**: Verify database hostname resolves correctly
5. **Database Overload**: Too many connections, database not responding
